passage: I write verses in the notebook under my bed. One I wrote in Class Eleven began, 'I'm a storm in a jar, and the jar is breaking.' I was angry about a fight with my parents, so I exaggerated it. When I read it aloud at the school slam poetry evening, some people in the audience stared, and one teacher, Mr Kamal, came up afterwards and asked quietly, "That was strong. Is that how you feel, or is it a character?" I said, "A bit of both. The storm is real, but I'm not going to break anything." He nodded. I liked that he asked instead of guessing. Poems let me shout on paper. Arohi.

qa.q: Where did Arohi read the verse aloud?
qa.a: Arohi read it at the school slam poetry evening.

qa.q: What did Mr Kamal want to know when he asked if it was a character?
qa.a: He wanted to understand whether the words described Arohi's real feelings or plans, or were a persona. He asked calmly instead of assuming.

qa.q: What would you advise a listener who hears a very dark lyric?
qa.a: Ask the writer kindly what it means, and take any talk of real harm seriously by getting help from a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might the audience members who stared have felt?
qa.a: Some may have been unsettled or moved, not knowing whether the words were real.

grounding: A teen writes verses using persona and exaggeration, and a listener asks the writer before assuming.

passage: Teacher's note, Monday. Kunal handed in the rap he'd written for the talent show. One verse said, 'I'll burn this whole town down, they never see me.' I felt uneasy and my first thought was to call his parents. Then I remembered that lyrics use exaggeration and persona, so I invited Bhavna, our counsellor, and Kunal to talk. Kunal explained, a little embarrassed, that the verse was about feeling invisible after his friends moved to another school, not about hurting anyone. He agreed to change the line, though he wanted to keep the 'invisible' image. Bhavna will check on how he's feeling about the friends. Class teacher.

qa.q: What did Kunal's verse say about the town?
qa.a: It said, 'I'll burn this whole town down, they never see me.'

qa.q: What was Kunal really feeling behind the line about the town?
qa.a: He was feeling invisible after his friends moved to another school, and the line was an exaggeration, not a plan. He was also a little embarrassed about being asked.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do next?
qa.a: Check on how he is coping with the lost friendships, and keep an open door for him to talk.

qa.q: How might the class teacher have felt on first reading Kunal's verse?
qa.a: The teacher felt uneasy and first thought of calling Kunal's parents, but then remembered that lyrics use exaggeration and chose a calm conversation instead.

grounding: A teen writes lyrics with exaggeration, and a caring adult asks the writer what the words mean.

passage:
Friday
I read my slam poem at the school open mic today. It's called "Ghost in the Canteen." It's about being new in this city and eating lunch alone. I made it big: "I am invisible, I am a rumour, I am the empty chair."
Afterwards Neelam Ma'am, the English teacher, found me by the water cooler. I thought she'd say "good job." Instead she said, "That was powerful. Can I ask how much of it is you, and how much is the poem?"
I liked that she asked instead of guessing. I told her the truth: I do eat alone sometimes, and I miss Chennai. But "invisible" is exaggeration. Poems need drama.
She nodded. "Thank you for telling me. The lunch part, would you like help with that? The book club meets at lunch on Tuesdays."
I might go. Maybe.
- Disha

qa.q: What was the slam poem called?
qa.a: "Ghost in the Canteen."

qa.q: What was Disha feeling about school life, based on the poem and the talk?
qa.a: Disha felt lonely at lunch and homesick for Chennai, though "invisible" was an exaggeration for the poem.

qa.q: What did Neelam Ma'am do well?
qa.a: She asked how much of the poem was real instead of assuming, then offered practical help with lunch through the book club.

qa.q: How might classmates who heard the poem have read it?
qa.a: Some may have taken every line as literal, thinking Disha felt completely invisible, without realising the persona and exaggeration.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager writing slam poetry with persona and exaggeration, and a teacher asking before assuming the words describe the writer's real life.

passage:
At the village school's annual function in Kalwan, Lokesh sang a song he had written himself, with Noor playing the dholak. The chorus went: "Girl by the river, with the silver bangle, I'll wait at the ghat till the moon is full."
The crowd loved it. By the next morning, half the school had decided it was about someone. Noor had a silver bangle. The teasing started immediately.
At the water tap, Noor asked him straight. "Is the song about me? People won't stop."
Lokesh looked horrified. "No! It's from my Aaji's story. She used to wait at the river for her friend, sixty years ago. I just made it sound romantic. Songs need that."
Noor laughed with relief. "You should tell people."
"I'll tell them it's about Aaji," he said. "That'll stop the teasing fast."
It did.

qa.q: Who played the dholak?
qa.a: Noor played the dholak.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she asked Lokesh at the water tap?
qa.a: Noor felt embarrassed and uneasy because of the teasing, and unsure whether the song was really about her.

qa.q: Which choice of Noor's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Lokesh directly worked, because the lyrics used a persona and an old family story, not his real feelings about her.

qa.q: How did the school read the song compared with what Lokesh meant?
qa.a: The school took the romantic lyrics as a real confession, while Lokesh had turned his grandmother's memory into a song.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager's song using persona and exaggeration, and a listener asking the writer before assuming the words are literal.

passage: At the youth centre's open mic in Lyon, Leila gripped the microphone stand and started low. "They cut the night bus, so we walk. / They cut the library hours, so we wait. / One day this whole grey city will burn / with everything we were never allowed to say." The last line came out as a shout, and the room erupted in snaps. Pablo, who had come to support her, clapped too, but a little slower. On the walk home he kept glancing at her. Finally he asked, "The burning part. That's... a picture, right? You're not planning anything?" Leila stared at him, then burst out laughing. "Pablo! It's a metaphor. The burning is us getting loud. I'm going to the council meeting on Thursday with a petition about the bus." He grinned, embarrassed. "Okay. Good. Sorry. It was just very convincing." "That's the job," she said, and bumped him with her bag.

qa.q: What did Leila's poem say was cut?
qa.a: The night bus and the library hours were cut.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when the last line came out as a shout?
qa.a: Leila was likely angry and frustrated about the cuts, and also exhilarated by performing; the shout was persona and exaggeration, not a real plan.

qa.q: Why was asking Leila better than deciding what the line meant?
qa.a: Lyrics use persona and exaggeration, so asking let Leila explain the metaphor and the real plan, a petition at Thursday's council meeting.

qa.q: What was it like for Pablo to hear the burning line?
qa.a: Pablo was uneasy and a little worried, clapping more slowly and asking on the walk home, then relieved and embarrassed when she explained.

grounding: It shows a teenager's slam poem using persona and exaggeration about injustice, and a listener asking before assuming the words describe real plans.
